clinicalPearls: Defined as a stretched penile length more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean for age in an otherwise normally formed penis with a correctly positioned urethral meatus
The normal structure but small size implies that androgen action was adequate during early urethral formation but deficient in the later gestational phase of penile growth
It is a sign rather than a diagnosis, most often reflecting hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, primary (hypergonadotropic) testicular failure, or partial defects in androgen synthesis or action
Measurement technique matters: the penis must be gently stretched with the suprapubic fat pad depressed, as a buried or concealed penis can mimic true micropenis
Associated hypoglycaemia or midline defects should raise concern for congenital hypopituitarism with multiple hormone deficiencies
A short trial of androgen therapy in infancy can both promote penile growth and provide diagnostic information about androgen responsiveness
Marked ambiguity of the genitalia points away from isolated micropenis and towards a disorder of sex development requiring karyotype and specialist assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Penile growth in the second half of gestation depends on testosterone secretion driven by fetal and placental gonadotropins and its conversion to dihydrotestosterone acting on androgen receptors. Because the urethra and overall penile architecture form earlier under androgen influence, a normally shaped but undersized penis indicates that androgen exposure was sufficient for structural development but inadequate during the later growth phase. The underlying defect may lie anywhere along the axis: deficient hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin drive (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), primary testicular failure with impaired testosterone production (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), or partial defects of testosterone biosynthesis or androgen-receptor signalling. In some cases no cause is identified and the finding is idiopathic.
additionalDifferentials: Buried or concealed penis (normal size obscured by suprapubic fat or skin)
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, including congenital GnRH deficiency and hypopituitarism
Defects of testosterone biosynthesis or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency
A more complex disorder of sex development
additionalInvestigations: Accurate stretched penile length measurement compared with age-based normative data
LH, FSH, and testosterone, ideally sampled during the neonatal minipuberty window
Assessment of the wider anterior pituitary axis (including cortisol, thyroid, and growth hormone) where hypopituitarism is suspected
hCG stimulation test to assess testicular testosterone production capacity
Karyotype and disorder-of-sex-development workup if there is any genital ambiguity
Pelvic and adrenal imaging where indicated by the hormonal findings
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, or midline facial defects suggesting congenital hypopituitarism
Bilateral non-palpable gonads or genital ambiguity indicating a possible disorder of sex development
Failure of any response to an appropriate androgen trial
Features suggesting adrenal insufficiency in a hypopituitary infant
reference.prognosis: Many infants respond to early androgen therapy with satisfactory penile growth and can expect adequate adult size and function; the overall outlook is dictated by the underlying cause, with fertility potential depending on whether the defect is central, gonadal, or in androgen action.
pitfalls: Diagnosing micropenis without a properly performed stretched measurement, mistaking a buried penis for a small one
Failing to evaluate the whole pituitary axis and missing life-threatening cortisol deficiency in hypopituitarism
Missing the neonatal minipuberty window, when hormonal evaluation is most informative
Overlooking an underlying disorder of sex development in the presence of subtle ambiguity
Attributing the finding to idiopathic causes before completing the endocrine assessment
management: Give a trial of androgen therapy (testosterone) in infancy to promote penile growth and gauge androgen responsiveness
Treat the underlying cause: gonadotrophin or GnRH therapy for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and testosterone induction of puberty for testicular failure
Where congenital hypopituitarism is present, replace deficient anterior pituitary hormones (glucocorticoid, thyroxine, growth hormone) and treat associated hypoglycaemia promptly
Monitor penile growth, overall growth pattern and pubertal progression over time
Provide psychological support to the family and, in due course, to the patient
Manage within a multidisciplinary paediatric and reproductive endocrinology and urology team, with disorder-of-sex-development input where there is genital ambiguity
Offer genetic counselling and karyotype or DSD assessment, and discuss fertility potential according to whether the defect is central, gonadal or in androgen action
